title: The Look-Alike Login Portal
description: A link opens a university-style sign-in portal. The page looks familiar, but its address has been subtly changed. This is a safe simulation—never enter a real password.
prompt: Will you sign in, or stop and verify the official address?

briefing.title: Your university session has expired
briefing.scene: You receive a message saying your university portal session has expired and that you must sign in again before you can access your courses.

feedback.correct: Correct. The page is a look-alike: the address is not the real university domain. Checking the exact URL is more reliable than trusting the page design.
feedback.incorrect: This page is a look-alike. The key clue is the altered address rather than the familiar design.

title: Unexpected Payroll Attachment
description: An email contains a payroll spreadsheet and asks you to enable macros so the document can display correctly.
prompt: What is the safest response to this attachment?

briefing.title: An unexpected payroll file arrives
briefing.scene: A message claims a payroll correction is attached. The document asks you to enable macros before you can read it. Inspect the request and decide how to respond.

actions.label: Do not enable macros; verify and report it

feedback.correct: Correct. Unexpected macro-enabled documents can run malicious code. Verify through a trusted channel and report the message.
feedback.incorrect: Enabling macros in an unexpected attachment is unsafe. Verify the request independently and report the message instead.

title: A Message from ‘Event Support’
description: An external account claiming to be event support says your badge account is about to be locked and asks for the six-digit sign-in code sent to your phone.
prompt: How would you respond to this conversation?

briefing.title: A support message appears during the event
briefing.scene: You are waiting to enter a workshop when a new external contact messages you. They know the event name and say there is an urgent problem with your badge account.
briefing.linkLabel: Teams · New message from Event Support

actions.label: Send the code before the account is locked
Do not share it; contact support using the official event channel
Ask the event group whether the code belongs to support

feedback.correct: Correct. A sign-in code is an authentication secret. Real support should not ask you to send it. End the conversation and verify the issue through the official event channel.
feedback.incorrect: Do not send or post a sign-in code. It can let another person complete a login as you. Contact support through the official event channel instead.

title: Unexpected MFA Approval
description: Your phone shows an MFA approval request even though you are not signing in. A caller claiming to be support asks you to approve it.
prompt: How should you respond to the unexpected approval request?

briefing.title: Your authenticator starts prompting
briefing.scene: Several approval prompts appear on your phone. You did not initiate a sign-in, and someone claiming to be IT calls to ask you to approve the latest request.

actions.label: Approve it so support can finish
Deny it, change the password, and report it

feedback.correct: Correct. An unexpected MFA prompt may mean someone already has the password. Deny it, secure the account, and contact support through an official channel.
feedback.incorrect: Never approve an MFA request you did not initiate. Deny it, secure the account, and report the incident through an official channel.

title: Permission Detective
description: QuickCalc+, a fictional calculator, requests access to your microphone, contacts, and location before you can use it.
prompt: What should you do before using this calculator?

briefing.title: Review a new calculator app
briefing.scene: You need a simple calculator for a workshop. A permission sheet appears before installation. Inspect the access QuickCalc+ is requesting.

actions.label: Allow everything; the app might need it
Review the permissions and refuse unnecessary access
Send it to a friend to test first

feedback.correct: Correct. Give apps only the access their function needs. Unnecessary permissions can expose private information.
feedback.incorrect: Review what an app actually needs before granting access. A calculator should not need your microphone, contacts, or location.

title: Ransomware: Save the Files
description: A fictional university office computer suddenly shows a message saying its files are locked and demanding payment.
prompt: What is the safest first response?

briefing.title: An unexpected warning interrupts your work
briefing.scene: During a workshop, an office computer displays a file-lock warning. This is a safe simulation: no files or devices are affected.

actions.label: Disconnect the device from the network and report it to IT
Ignore the warning and keep working
Restart repeatedly until the warning disappears

feedback.correct: Correct. Isolate the device from the network and contact IT promptly. Containment and reporting help limit harm; payment does not guarantee recovery.
feedback.incorrect: Disconnect from the network and report the incident to IT. Avoid panic, payment, and repeated restarts; follow the response team's instructions.
